people.narrative: Richard Bissell is where the documented record of Area 51 begins, and the board's Nevada material has until now had no origin point. The CIA's own History Staff monograph, in its fuller 2013 release, records that Allen Dulles put him in charge of the U-2 project on 26 November 1954; that on 12 April 1955 he flew over Nevada with Osmund Ritland, Kelly Johnson and Tony LeVier and spotted the airstrip at Groom Lake; that on finding it lay outside the AEC's proving ground he asked the Commission to absorb it, which Chairman Lewis Strauss agreed to and Eisenhower approved; and that the strip's map designation was Area 51. The same monograph records that Blue Book investigators checked their UFO reports against the project's flight logs and were not permitted to tell correspondents the cause. Nothing in it touches the deathbed briefing claim the Michels corpus routes through him, and that claim must not travel with this node.

people.narrative: Walter Bedell Smith is the Director of Central Intelligence whose own instruction, on 20 August 1952, turned unidentified flying objects from an Air Force nuisance into an intelligence-community problem with a draft National Security Council directive behind it. Chadwell's memoranda run to him, name him as the approving authority on the recommendation that the DCI take the subject to the Psychological Strategy Board, and attach a memorandum to the NSC Executive Secretary over his signature block proposing a coordinated research programme. The Agency's own later correspondence states plainly that the Robertson Panel 'was convened at the direction of General Smith'. The board carries the Robertson Panel at 112 occurrences and has one occurrence of his name; he is the office from which it issued. The Michels corpus describes a 1953 Bedell Smith letter proposing psychological warfare; the psychological-warfare document is Chadwell's, dated 2 October 1952, the approval line over Smith's name on the released copy is blank, and Smith's own 2 December 1952 draft proposes research rather than exploitation.
people.tierRationale: C, A and D carried from the verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-michels-5.md section 3, draft node A.

claims.text: Smith personally started the intelligence-community effort. Chadwell's 2 December 1952 memorandum to the DCI opens: 'On 20 August, the DCI, after a briefing by OSI on the above subject, directed the preparation of an NSCID for submission to the Council stating the need for investigation and directing agencies concerned to cooperate in such investigations.'
claims.source: H. Marshall Chadwell, Memorandum for Director of Central Intelligence, subject: Unidentified Flying Objects, 2 December 1952, CIA document C00015340, para. 1, https://archive.org/details/cia-readingroom-document-0005515935

claims.text: A memorandum to the National Security Council was drafted over his name proposing research, not exploitation: 'It is my view that this situation has possible implications for our national security which transcend the interests of a single service. A broader, coordinated effort should be initiated to develop a firm scientific understanding of the several phenomena which apparently are involved in these reports, and to assure ourselves that the incidents will not hamper our present efforts in the Cold War or confuse our early warning system in case of an attack.' The typed signature block reads 'Walter B. Smith / Director'.
claims.source: Draft Memorandum to the Executive Secretary, National Security Council, subject: Unidentified Flying Objects (Flying Saucers), attached to CIA document C00015340, 2 December 1952, para. 2, https://archive.org/details/cia-readingroom-document-0005515935

claims.text: He is named as the approving authority on the recommendation that the DCI take the subject to the Psychological Strategy Board, and on the released copy the approval was never recorded. The 2 October 1952 routing page reads 'ACTION BY APPROVING AUTHORITY: Date: ____ Approved (disapproved): ____ WALTER B. SMITH, Director'; both lines are blank. The recommendation itself is action (b): 'That the DCI discuss this subject with the Psychological Strategy Board. A memorandum to the Director, Psychological Strategy Board, is attached for signature as TAB C.'
claims.source: H. Marshall Chadwell, Memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence, subject: Flying Saucers, 2 October 1952, CIA document C00015339, para. 4 and routing page, https://archive.org/details/cia-readingroom-document-0005515933

claims.text: The CIA attributed the Robertson Panel to him in writing. Allen W. Dulles, transmitting the panel report on 13 March 1953: 'This panel was convened at the direction of General Smith, following the recommendation of the Intelligence Advisory Committee.'

people.narrative: Allen W. Dulles signed the three letters that closed the Agency's 1952 flying-saucer file. On 13 March 1953, over his name and on Office of the Director paper classified SECRET, the CIA sent the Robertson Panel report to the Secretary of Defense, to the Federal Civil Defense Administration and to the National Security Resources Board, told each that the conclusions pointed to 'certain potential dangers to national security', and then said in the same letter that the Agency did not consider the subject primarily its concern. Those three letters do two things the board needs: they attribute the panel to Bedell Smith in the Agency's own words, and they are a dated, signed instance of the Agency stepping back from a subject it had itself convened a panel on ten weeks earlier. Dulles also has an OSS personnel file, named by the National Archives among the notable files opened in 2008; the board carries no Office of Strategic Services node, so no edge is drawn for it.

claims.text: On 13 March 1953 Dulles forwarded the Robertson Panel report to three agencies over his own signature, describing it as pointing out 'certain potential dangers to national security which are related to the subject and suggest ways of their elimination.' claims.text: The same letters distance the Agency from the subject in the same breath: 'Although this Agency does not consider problems arising from sightings of "flying saucers" primarily its concern, we shall be pleased to assist in any appropriate action that you deem advisable.'

entities.label: Atomic Energy Commission
entities.sub: Civilian atomic authority, 1946-1974; statutory custodian of fissionable material and atomic weapons
entities.desc: The Atomic Energy Commission was created by the Atomic Energy Act of 1946 and took statutory title to everything the Manhattan Engineer District had held: all fissionable material, all atomic weapons and parts, and all processes and technical information behind them. It ran the born-secret information regime, under which data in defined categories is classified by operation of statute and declassified only by an affirmative act of the Commission, and it gated every contractor employee's access behind an FBI investigation and a Commission determination. Its Division of Military Application was established in the founding statute and directed by a serving officer of the armed forces. The Energy Reorganization Act of 1974 abolished it and vested its functions in ERDA, from which they passed to the Department of Energy. Four guests across four Michels lead maps place the Commission at a custody point for recovered material; nothing in either statute or in the National Archives record group description says anything about recovered material, and the node carries the statute rather than the testimony.
entities.tierRationale: C, A and D carried from the verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-michels-1.md section 1.

claims.text: The Commission was created by statute: 'There is hereby established an Atomic Energy Commission (herein called the Commission), which shall be composed of five members.' Members are appointed by the President by and with the advice and consent of the Senate.
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, sec. 2(a), approved 1 August 1946, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: The Commission took statutory custody of the Manhattan Engineer District's holdings. Section 9(a) directs the transfer to the Commission of 'All fissionable material; all atomic weapons and parts thereof' and of 'Such other property owned by or in the custody or control of the Manhattan Engineer District or other Government agencies as the President may determine.'
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, sec. 9(a), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: Classification runs by category rather than by decision. The 1946 Act defines restricted data as 'all data concerning the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons, the production of fissionable material, or the use of fissionable material in the production of power, but shall not include any data which the Commission from time to time determines may be published without adversely affecting the common defense and security.'
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, sec. 10(b)(1), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: A Division of Military Application under a serving officer was in the Commission from the start: the 1946 Act establishes it alongside Research, Production and Engineering and provides that 'The Director of the Division of Military Application shall be a member of the armed forces.' The 1954 Act carries it forward at section 25 with the Director required to be 'an active member of the Armed Forces.'

claims.text: The Commission was abolished by statute: 'The Atomic Energy Commission is hereby abolished.' Its functions vested in the Administrator of the Energy Research and Development Administration, and the Act took effect 120 days after enactment or on an earlier date the President might prescribe.

entities.label: Bluegill Triple Prime
entities.sub: FISHBOWL high-altitude shot, Operation DOMINIC I, Johnston Island, 25 October 1962
entities.desc: Bluegill Triple Prime was the fourth attempt to detonate the BLUEGILL device above Johnston Island, and the first that worked. Three earlier attempts failed: the 2 June 1962 launch was destroyed in flight after tracking was lost, BLUEGILL Prime burned on the pad, and BLUEGILL Double Prime failed on 15 October. The successful shot is recorded by the Defense Nuclear Agency at 25 October 1962, 2359 local, submegaton, tens of kilometres over Johnston Island, with 22 Air Force aircraft arrayed and nine Navy ships positioned to gather data. Four guests across four Michels lead maps attach a recovery story to it, and the record contradicts them in three places at once. The date is 25 October in the report's narrative and in its own Table 1, not 26 October, which is the GMT rendering of the same instant. DNA 6039F, cited for the shot in the candidates row, is Operation ARGUS 1958 and not the FISHBOWL report at all. And the report contains no unidentified object, no recovery, no debris, no RC-135 and no Cobra Ball: what it does carry is the call sign KETTLE, assigned to three KC-135 photographic aircraft, which is the documented origin of the Kettle film names the corpus uses. The node exists to hold the documented event so that the testimony has something dated to hang from.
entities.tierRationale: C, A and D carried from the verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-michels-1.md section 2.

claims.text: Its place in the test series, from the report's own summary table: '25 Oct / BLUE GILL / FISHBOWL shot, submegaton, tens of kilometers over Johnston Island', sourced there to Announced United States Nuclear Tests, NVO-29 (Rev. 1), Department of Energy, Nevada Operations Office, January 1980.

claims.text: The force present: 'The Air Force arrayed 22 aircraft for the detonation', with WB-50 and U-2 weather aircraft, Navy P2Vs for surveillance and pod recovery and Marine helicopters, and nine Navy ships positioned to gather scientific data.
claims.source: DNA 6040F, narrative for BLUEGILL Triple Prime, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA136820/DTIC_ADA136820_djvu.txt

claims.text: KETTLE is a DOMINIC aircraft call sign, not a film. The aircraft participation table lists '3 / KC-135 / Kettle / Photographic aircraft' alongside Cognac, Kibosh, Cordova, Caboodle, Abusive, Lambkin, Baxter/Byron, Hewstone and White Spot. The strings 'RC-135' and 'Cobra' do not appear anywhere in the report.

claims.text: The report contains nothing of what is attached to this shot. It carries no reference to any unidentified object, unknown craft, anomalous observation, recovery or debris associated with the detonation; its only uses of 'unidentified' are an unidentified number of dosimetry analyses and one unidentified event in a fallout discussion. 'Gise' appears zero times in it, and so does Malmgren's name.

In November 1997 it agreed to acquire BDM International through a cash tender offer at $29.50 a share, and BDM deregistered a month later. On 11 December 2002 TRW was itself merged into a Northrop Grumman subsidiary, with TRW surviving as a wholly owned subsidiary; TRW Systems became Northrop Grumman Mission Systems at Reston and TRW Space and Electronics became Northrop Grumman Space Technology at Redondo Beach. EDGAR carries the same transition on the company's own CIK. Until now the board reached from BDM to Northrop Grumman with no node in between, and the edge was an assertion where the filings make it a record. The corpus's further claim, that TRW was the parent of an unnamed FFRDC that ran the programme for about 29 years, is supported by nothing in any filing opened here.

entities.label: Invention Secrecy Act of 1951 (Pub. L. 82-256, 66 Stat. 3), codified at 35 U.S.C. 181-188
entities.sub: Act of 1 February 1952, ch. 4; renumbered by the Patent Act of 19 July 1952, ch. 950, 66 Stat. 805
entities.desc: The statute that lets the United States order an invention kept secret and withhold the patent, including an invention the government does not own and did not fund. It is the instrument the board's PATENTS tab is arguing around, and until now the board named it once in prose and carried no node for it. Its short title, printed in the margin of the Statutes at Large, is the Invention Secrecy Act of 1951, although the Act was approved on 1 February 1952; the familiar 35 U.S.C. 181-188 numbering comes from a different statute five months later, the Patent Act of 19 July 1952. Section 181's second paragraph routes a privately owned application to the Atomic Energy Commission and the Secretary of Defense for inspection before any order issues, which is the point at which the patent record and the weapons establishment touch. Orders run one year and renew annually without limit; the Patent and Trademark Office reported 6,543 in force at the end of fiscal 2025.
entities.tierRationale: The verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-michels-2.md section 6 gave no C, A or D. Reasoned from the opened statute: C 0 because the Act holds no material; A 2 because section 181 gives the Atomic Energy Commission and the Secretary of Defense a statutory right to inspect a privately owned application; D 1 because the Act is an instrument of withholding rather than of forcing the record open, and the only public series about its use is the count FAS obtains from the Patent and Trademark Office.

claims.text: The Act's own short title and date: the Statutes at Large prints the marginal note 'Invention Secrecy Act of 1951.' beside section 1 of 'Public Law 256', 'CHAPTER 4', an Act 'To provide for the withholding of certain patents that might be detrimental to the national security, and for other purposes', approved 'February 1, 1952 [H.R.4687]'.
claims.source: 66 Stat. 3, Statutes at Large volume 66, govinfo, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-66/pdf/STATUTE-66-Pg3.pdf

claims.text: The current codification descends from that Act by way of a second one. The Historical and Revision Notes to 35 U.S.C. 181 read: 'Based on Title 35, U.S.C., 1946 ed., 151 (Feb. 1, 1952, ch. 4, 1, 66 Stat. 3, 4).' The section's source credit is 'July 19, 1952, ch. 950, 66 Stat. 805'.
claims.source: 35 U.S.C. 181, Office of the Law Revision Counsel, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title35-section181&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: The Act reaches inventions the government does not own. Section 181 second paragraph: where the Commissioner of Patents believes disclosure of an invention 'in which the Government does not have a property interest' might be detrimental to the national security, 'he shall make the application for patent in which such invention is disclosed available for inspection to the Atomic Energy Commission, the Secretary of Defense, and the chief officer of any other department or agency of the Government designated by the President as a defense agency of the United States.'
claims.source: 35 U.S.C. 181, Office of the Law Revision Counsel, https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title35-section181&num=0&edition=prelim

claims.text: An order is indefinite by renewal, and wartime orders outlast the war. Section 181: 'An invention shall not be ordered kept secret and the publication of the application or the grant of a patent withheld for a period of more than one year', renewable annually on an affirmative determination that 'the national interest continues so to require'; an order in effect during a time when the United States is at war 'shall remain in effect for the duration of hostilities and one year following cessation of hostilities.'

entities.label: DoD Nuclear Weapon Personnel Reliability Program (DoD Directive 5210.42)
entities.sub: DoDD 5210.42, 25 May 1993, ASD(C3I); reissues the directive of 6 December 1985
entities.desc: The published rule that decides whether a person on a nuclear weapons site keeps his access, and the reason the board can treat 'they were afraid to report' as something other than an anecdote. The directive opened here is the 25 May 1993 edition, distribution unlimited, which reissues an edition of 6 December 1985; the current manual could not be reached from this environment and nothing here should be read as describing it. Its force for this board is not what it says about UFOs, which is nothing, but what it says about who may find a person unreliable and on what evidence: a non-medical certifying official, with access to the individual's medical record without his consent, may act on 'aberrant behavior' or on mood described as unusual happiness, sadness or agitation. Every witness at a nuclear site whose testimony this board carries was subject to a rule of that shape. Two things the corpus attaches to the programme are not in the directive: the duty to report an over-the-counter analgesic, and the figure 167, which is Robert Hastings's count of nuclear-base witnesses rather than a count of PRP personnel.
entities.tierRationale: The verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-michels-2.md section 7 gave no C, A or D. Reasoned from the opened directive: C 1 because it governs personnel at nuclear weapons sites, which is adjacent to the board's custody locations but not to any recovered material; A 2 because the directive is itself an access-control regime for nuclear weapons duty; D 0 because it plays no part in forcing the record open and the board's use of it is as a mechanism of silence.

claims.text: Scope and purpose: the directive applies to 'DoD military and civilian personnel and contractor employees assigned to PRP positions or in training leading to assignment to PRP positions', and exists to 'ensure the highest possible standards of individual reliability in personnel performing duties associated with nuclear weapons and critical components.'
claims.source: DoD Directive 5210.42, 25 May 1993, sections A and B, DTIC AD-A271698, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA271698/DTIC_ADA271698_djvu.txt

claims.text: Disqualification reaches demeanour, not only conduct. Under 'Poor Attitude or Lack of Motivation' the directive lists 'aberrant attitude (arrogance, inflexibility, or suspiciousness), behavior (impulsiveness, destructiveness, or suicide threats), or mood (unusual happiness, sadness, or agitation).'
claims.source: DoD Directive 5210.42, 25 May 1993, enclosure 4, DTIC AD-A271698, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA271698/DTIC_ADA271698_djvu.txt

claims.text: The medical file is open to the chain without consent: 'medical records may be disclosed to reviewing and certifying officials for this purpose without either a request from, or the consent of, the individuals to whom those records pertain', and the health record is 'marked to reflect assignment of an individual to a PRP position'.
claims.source: DoD Directive 5210.42, 25 May 1993, enclosure 4, DTIC AD-A271698, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA271698/DTIC_ADA271698_djvu.txt

claims.text: The programme runs on self-reporting and peer review. The certifying official's personal interview must inform the individual of 'the individual's responsibility for self-reporting and peer review of factors and situations that could adversely affect job performance or reliability.'
claims.source: DoD Directive 5210.42, 25 May 1993, enclosure 4, DTIC AD-A271698, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA271698/DTIC_ADA271698_djvu.txt

claims.text: Speakers on the American Alchemy corpus describe PRP as a reason nuclear-site personnel did not report what they saw, and attach a figure of 167 to it. The 167 is Robert Hastings's count of nuclear-base witnesses, not a count of PRP personnel; no opened record supports either the figure or the reporting claim, and the directive contains no provision about reporting aerial phenomena.

entities.label: Manned Orbiting Laboratory and the DORIAN / KH-10 reconnaissance payload
entities.sub: USAF programme with an NRO black mission; announced December 1963, cancelled 10 June 1969, declassified October 2015
entities.desc: A fully documented case of a real programme carrying a second, classified programme inside it, closed by the government and then released by the agency that ran it. Publicly MOL was an Air Force laboratory to determine the military usefulness of men in space; inside it sat DORIAN, an NRO reconnaissance system handled in the BYEMAN control system and designated KH-10 in 1969. Seventeen officers were astronaut-trained between 1965 and 1969, on a modified Gemini-B with a hatch through the heat shield, for polar launches from Vandenberg on the Titan-IIIM. None of them flew. The programme was cancelled on 10 June 1969 with 13,187 cleared contractor personnel on it, and the NRO declassified almost the entire DORIAN collection in October 2015. It is the strongest available answer to a question this board is repeatedly asked, which is what a secret space programme actually looks like on the record. Two opened sources disagree on one number and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved: the NRO volume gives a 70-inch aperture and NASA gives a 72-inch diameter primary mirror.
entities.tierRationale: The verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-michels-2.md section 8 gave no C, A or D, and used the cluster 'programs', which is not in the board's vocabulary. Cluster set to 'ic' because the classified half of the programme was the NRO's. Reasoned from the opened record: C 1 because no opened record connects the programme to recovered material; A 3 because DORIAN was handled inside the BYEMAN control system, which is the compartmented special access this axis measures; D 2 because the October 2015 release of over 850 documents is one of the board's clearest instances of a closed programme entering the public record.

claims.text: The cover and the mission are described by the agency itself. The NRO's volume says MOL was 'open "white" world, but maintained a highly-classified "black" mission', with the reconnaissance mission 'codenamed Dorian in the BYEMAN security system', and its foreword calls Dorian 'a deeply classified program managed by the then darkly hidden agency of the Intelligence Community, the National Reconnaissance Office'.

claims.text: The declassification is dated and quantified in the NRO's own words: on 22 October 2015 the CSNR held a panel at the National Museum of the United States Air Force 'on the occasion of the NRO declassifying almost its entire collection of records on the Dorian program. There were over 850 documents with some 22,000 pages and 280 photographs.'
claims.source: Spies in Space, NRO CSNR, May 2019, foreword, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652/pdf/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652.pdf

claims.text: Seventeen officers were trained and none flew: 'Between 1965 and 1969, quietly and without fanfare, 17 non-NASA individuals were astronaut-trained in order to meet the reconnaissance needs of the United States.' entities.label: TR-AC-47, Joint ATIC-WADC Report on Project Silver Bug, 15 February 1955
entities.sub: Air Technical Intelligence Center, Wright-Patterson AFB; Project No. 9961; declassified 29 March 1995
entities.desc: A joint report of the Air Technical Intelligence Center and the Wright Air Development Center on a Canadian contractor's proposal for a supersonic circular-planform aircraft with vertical take-off. It is the cleanest documented instance on this board of the Air Force funding a disc-shaped aircraft at Wright-Patterson, and its own stated purpose is to stop the intelligence community from believing the exaggerated accounts already circulating about it. It is the control case any Wright-Patterson recovery claim has to clear, and it is cited in the Michels corpus for the opposite of what it says: the transcript frames the project as a funnel and cover for deeper theoretical physics, while the report exists 'to correct the distorted picture presented in previous releases, both classified and unclassified' and says the project 'should in no way be associated with any science fiction or "Flying Saucer" stories because of its external appearance'. John Frost is named nowhere in it, the report names no individual designer at all, and the contractor is A. V. Roe, Canada, Limited, of the Hawker-Siddley Group, not the British Aircraft Corporation, which did not exist in 1955.

entities.label: Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities (Church Committee)
entities.sub: Established by S. Res. 21, 27 January 1975; final report S. Rept. 94-755, six books, 1976
entities.desc: The only thorough congressional investigation ever made of the United States intelligence system, and the benchmark this board's oversight view has lacked. Eleven senators, a hundred staff, more than eight hundred interviews and over a hundred and ten thousand pages of documents. It is carried here for what its own final report concedes rather than for what it achieved: that it never once examined an agency's files on its own, that the CIA and other executive agencies limited its access to the record, and that three chapters of its published findings, including the chapter on budgetary oversight, were deleted at the request of the agencies it was investigating. Two Michels-corpus speakers who agree on almost nothing else, Michael Shellenberger and Mick West, each name the committee as the template for a successful congressional penetration of a compartmented programme. The committee's own report says the penetration was mediated throughout, and that is the finding.

entities.label: Atomic Energy Act of 1946 (McMahon Act)
entities.sub: Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, 1 August 1946; the origin of born-secret classification
entities.desc: The Atomic Energy Act of 1946 is where classification by category enters United States law. It defines restricted data as an entire class of fact rather than as a set of documents somebody decided to mark, makes publication conditional on an affirmative determination by the Atomic Energy Commission, and backs the rule with a capital penalty that reaches concealment and destruction as well as disclosure. It gates every contractor employee's access behind an FBI investigation and a Commission finding, gives the FBI exclusive jurisdiction over violations, and gives the War and Navy Departments a standing consultative claim over the control of weapons information through the Military Liaison Committee, with an appeal that ends at the President. The board argues the 1954 Act's Restricted Data regime is the statutory shield; this is the instrument that built it, a year before the programme's own 1947 start. The popular name McMahon Act appears in no federal record opened for this node; what is documented is Brien McMahon's chairmanship of the Senate Special Committee on Atomic Energy and of the Joint Committee on Atomic Energy in the 79th Congress.
entities.tierRationale: C, A and D carried from the verifier's draft in research/leads/verified-michels-5.md section 1. The draft used the person field 'date'; on the entity shape this is dateStart, and dateEnd is left null because the Act was superseded rather than repealed on a date the opened record states.

claims.text: The Act's own short title is narrow: 'This Act may be cited as the "Atomic Energy Act of 1946".' The chapter head gives it as Chapter 724, S. 1717, Public Law 585, 79th Congress, 'AN ACT For the development and control of atomic energy', approved August 1, 1946. The popular name 'McMahon Act' appears nowhere in the statute.
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, sec. 21 and chapter head, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: Classification runs by category, and publication is the exception. Section 10(b)(1): restricted data 'means all data concerning the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons, the production of fissionable material, or the use of fissionable material in the production of power, but shall not include any data which the Commission from time to time determines may be published without adversely affecting the common defense and security.' Section 10(a) makes it 'the policy of the Commission to control the dissemination of restricted data in such a manner as to assure the common defense and security.'
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 10(a) and 10(b)(1), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: The penalty reaches concealment and destruction, not only disclosure, and it is capital. Section 10(b)(4) provides that whoever 'removes, conceals, tampers with, alters, mutilates, or destroys' a document incorporating restricted data with intent to injure the United States 'shall be punished by death or imprisonment for life (but the penalty of death or imprisonment for life may be imposed only upon recommendation of the jury and only in cases where the offense was committed with intent to injure the United States); or by a fine of not more than $20,000 or imprisonment for not more than twenty years, or both.'
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 10(b)(4), and identically at 10(b)(2)(A) and 10(b)(3), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: The FBI is both the gate and the investigator. Section 10(b)(5)(B)(i) bars any arrangement, contract or licence unless the contractor 'agrees in writing not to permit any individual to have access to restricted data until the Federal Bureau of Investigation shall have made an investigation and report to the Commission on the character, associations, and loyalty of such individual.' Section 10(b)(5)(C): 'All violations of this Act shall be investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation of the Department of Justice.'
claims.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, sec. 10(b)(5)(B)(i) and 10(b)(5)(C), https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

claims.text: The military keeps a standing claim over the control of weapons information, with an appeal that ends at the President. timeline.label: Atomic Energy Act of 1946 makes classification a property of a category
timeline.text: Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, chapter 724, S. 1717, is approved. Section 10(b)(1) defines restricted data as all data concerning the manufacture or utilization of atomic weapons, the production of fissionable material or its use in the production of power, excluding only what the Commission affirmatively determines may be published. Section 2(a) establishes the Atomic Energy Commission, section 9(a) transfers the Manhattan Engineer District's holdings to it, section 10(b)(4) reaches concealment and destruction with a capital penalty, and section 10(b)(5)(C) gives the FBI exclusive jurisdiction over violations.
timeline.source: Atomic Energy Act of 1946, Public Law 79-585, 60 Stat. 755, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/STATUTE-60/pdf/STATUTE-60-Pg755.pdf

timeline.label: ATIC and WADC report jointly on a disc-shaped supersonic aircraft
timeline.text: TR-AC-47, Project No. 9961, is issued at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base on the Avro Canada Project Y2 flat-riser. Its stated purpose is to correct the distorted picture presented in previous releases and to alert the intelligence community to any Soviet interest, and its Summary says the project should in no way be associated with any science fiction or flying saucer stories because of its external appearance. It was declassified on 29 March 1995.
timeline.source: TR-AC-47, Joint ATIC-WADC Report on Project Silver Bug, 15 February 1955, https://documents.theblackvault.com/documents/SilverBug/AFD-070114-006.pdf

timeline.label: NICAP incorporated in the District of Columbia
timeline.text: The National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena states in its own 1964 volume that it is a non-profit organization incorporated in the District of Columbia in 1956. A Washington Daily News report of 23 October 1956, filed in the FBI's NICAP file, records the organisation forming at 1536 Connecticut Avenue NW under T. Townsend Brown of Leesburg, Virginia, executive vice chairman pro tempore, with a nine-man board of governors still to be elected on 1 November. The District's own corporate register was not opened.
timeline.source: The UFO Evidence, NICAP, May 1964, CIA filed copy CIA-RDP81R00560R000100010001-0, https://archive.org/details/cia-readingroom-document-cia-rdp81r00560r000100010001-0 ; FBI file 100-35992, part 1, https://archive.org/details/NICAP

timeline.label: A Study of Lunar Research Flights delivered to the Air Force Special Weapons Center
timeline.text: AFSWC TR-59-39 Vol I, by L. Reiffel of the Armour Research Foundation with contributions including C. E. Sagan, is dated 19 June 1959 under Contract AF 29(601)-1164. Its introduction states that the motivation for detonating a nuclear weapon on or near the Moon is threefold, scientific, military and political, and that positive effects would accrue to the nation first performing the feat. Copies went to ARPA at the Pentagon, to the AEC for the Division of Military Application, to Sandia, to Los Alamos, to the Lawrence Radiation Laboratory and to WADD at Wright-Patterson. The string A119 appears nowhere in it.
timeline.source: AFSWC TR-59-39 Vol I, DDC AD 425380, https://archive.org/details/DTIC_AD0425380

timeline.label: Bluegill Triple Prime detonates over Johnston Island
timeline.text: The Defense Nuclear Agency's Operation DOMINIC I report records the shot at 25 October 1962, 2359 local, the fourth and first successful attempt to launch the BLUEGILL device on a Thor missile, submegaton, tens of kilometres over Johnston Island, with 22 Air Force aircraft arrayed and nine Navy ships positioned. The report carries no unidentified object, no recovery and no debris, and the photographic aircraft were three KC-135s under the call sign KETTLE.
timeline.source: DNA 6040F, Operation DOMINIC I--1962, Defense Nuclear Agency, https://archive.org/download/DTIC_ADA136820/DTIC_ADA136820_djvu.txt

timeline.label: Church Committee files Book I and records that it never examined an agency file itself
timeline.text: Senate Report 94-755, Book I, Foreign and Military Intelligence, is filed. Its section on the obstacles the committee met states that despite its legal Senate mandate and the issuance of subpoenas, in no instance had the committee been able to examine the agencies' files on its own. Its publication note records that three chapters, Cover, Espionage and Budgetary Oversight, were deleted at the request of the agencies.

timeline.label: NRO declassifies almost the entire DORIAN collection
timeline.text: The NRO's Center for the Study of National Reconnaissance held a panel at the National Museum of the United States Air Force on the occasion of the NRO declassifying almost its entire collection of records on the Dorian program: over 850 documents with some 22,000 pages and 280 photographs. Line-by-line review had taken over a year, and the collection was posted on the NRO public web page the day after the panel.
timeline.source: Spies in Space: Reflections on National Reconnaissance and the Manned Orbiting Laboratory, NRO CSNR, May 2019, foreword, https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652/pdf/GOVPUB-D-PURL-gpo123652.pdf
